import sys, re
text = '''
fracture risk PHYSIOTHERAPY Resistance exercises Weight bearing activities Balance training Postural exercises Gait training 
Fall prevention Functional strengthening --- 15 OSTEOPOROSIS DEFINITION Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder 
characterized by reduced bone strength resulting from low bone mass and/ or deterioration of bone microarchitecture and 
consequently an increased risk of fragility fractures TYPES 1 Primary osteoporosis Type I Postmenopausal osteoporosis Type 
II Age related/senile osteoporosis 2 Secondary osteoporosis Due to Endocrine disorders Chronic kidney disease 
Malabsorption Rheumatological disease Medications especially glucocorticoids Prolonged immobilization Nutritional 
disorders RISK FACTORS • Non modifiable Increasing age Female sex Previous fragility fracture Family history Menopause • 
Modifiable Smoking Excessive alcohol Physical inactivity Poor calcium/vitamin D intake Low body weight Prolonged 
immobilization • Drug related Long term glucocorticoids Some anticonvulsants Certain hormonal 
therapies PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Bone resorption exceeds bone formation ↓ Loss of bone mass ↓ Trabecular thinning and 
cortical porosity ↓ Reduced bone strength ↓ Fragility fracture CLINICAL FEATURES Often called a silent disease because 
bone loss may occur without symptoms until fracture develops Manifestations Back pain Vertebral compression fracture 
Loss of height Kyphosis Fragility fracture Hip Wrist Vertebrae Difficulty walking Reduced independence INVESTIGATIONS • 
DXA scan Standard test for bone mineral density T score thresholds apply -1 0 Normal -1 0 to -2 5 Osteopenia -2 5 
Osteoporosis • Blood investigations Calcium Phosphate ALP Vitamin D Renal function Thyroid studies to identify secondary 
causes • X ray Fractures Vertebral compression Kyphosis COMPLICATIONS Vertebral compression fracture Hip fracture 
Wrist fracture Loss of height Kyphosis Chronic pain Reduced mobility Falls Loss of independence Increased mortality 
following major hip fracture MEDICAL MANAGEMENT 1 Lifestyle management Adequate calcium and vitamin D Weight 
bearing and resistance exercise Balance training Smoking cessation Limit excessive alcohol Fall prevention 2 
Pharmacological treatment Bisphosphonates Denosumab Selective estrogen receptor modulators Anabolic agents 
teriparatide/abaloparatide Romosozumab Choice depends on fracture risk age renal function previous fractures 
contraindications SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Osteoporosis itself is usually managed medically Surgery is required for 
complications e g fracture management via internal fixation arthroplasty vertebral augmentation for vertebral compression 
hemiarthroplasty/THA for hip fractures PHYSIOTHERAPY MANAGEMENT Goals Improve muscle strength Improve balance 
Prevent falls Maintain posture Improve functional independence Reduce fracture risk Exercises Weight bearing exercise 
Resistance training Back extensor strengthening Balance training Postural exercises Gait training Precautions Avoid high 
impact activity in patients at high fracture risk Forceful spinal flexion Excessive twisting Unsupervised heavy lifting //
/// 1 OSTEOARTHRITIS DEFINITION Osteoarthritis OA is a chronic progressive degenerative disorder of synovial joints 
characterized by loss of articular cartilage subchondral bone changes osteophyte formation and varying degrees of synovial 
inflammation resulting in pain stiffness and functional limitation CAUSES / RISK FACTORS Primary OA Occurs without a 
single identifiable cause Risk factors • Increasing age • Female sex • Obesity • Genetic predisposition • Previous joint injury 
• Repetitive joint loading Secondary OA Occurs due to an identifiable condition • Previous fracture • Joint infection • 
Rheumatoid arthritis • Congenital joint abnormality • Ligament injury • Meniscal injury • Avascular necrosis • Metabolic 
disorders COMMON SITES • Knee • Hip • Spine • Hands • First MTP joint • Shoulder and other joints less 
commonly PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Mechanical/biological stress ↓ Cartilage matrix degeneration ↓ Loss of proteoglycans and 
collagen integrity ↓ Cartilage thinning and fissuring ↓ Subchondral sclerosis ↓ Osteophyte formation ↓ Joint space 
narrowing ↓ Pain + stiffness + deformity CLINICAL FEATURES Symptoms • Joint pain usually worse with activity • Pain 
relieved by rest initially • Morning stiffness usually less than 30 minutes • Stiffness after prolonged inactivity • Difficulty 
walking • Difficulty climbing stairs • Reduced functional activity Signs • Joint tenderness • Crepitus • Reduced ROM • Bony 
enlargement • Joint line tenderness • Muscle weakness • Deformity in advanced disease Hand OA • Heberdens nodes DIP 
joints • Bouchards nodes PIP joints DEFORMITIES Knee • Varus deformity • Valgus deformity Hip • Flexion deformity • 
External rotation • Adduction deformity Hands • Heberdens and Bouchards nodes RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES X ray shows • 
Non uniform joint space narrowing • Osteophytes • Subchondral sclerosis • Subchondral cysts • Bony remodeling • 
Deformity in advanced disease Classic mnemonic LOSS • Loss of joint space • Osteophytes • Subchondral sclerosis • 
Subchondral cysts COMPLICATIONS • Severe pain • Joint deformity • Contractures • Muscle wasting • Reduced mobility • 
Disability • Secondary instability • Reduced quality of life CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Medical • Patient education • 
Weight reduction • Activity modification • Paracetamol/analgesics where appropriate • NSAIDs when appropriate • Topical 
NSAIDs • Intra articular corticosteroid injection in selected cases • Management of comorbidities Physiotherapy • ROM 
exercises • Quadriceps strengthening • Hip strengthening • Aerobic exercise • Aquatic exercise • Gait training • Balance 
exercises • Assistive devices • Bracing when indicated SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Indicated in severe symptomatic disease 
with significant functional limitation despite conservative treatment Procedures • Arthroscopic procedures in selected 
circumstances • Osteotomy in selected younger patients with appropriate deformity • Total knee replacement • Total hip 
replacement • Other joint replacement procedures --- 2 RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS DEFINITION Rheumatoid arthritis RA is a 
chronic systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized primarily by persistent inflammatory synovitis of 
multiple joints leading to cartilage destruction bone erosion deformity and extra articular manifestations CAUSES / RISK 
FACTORS Exact cause is unknown Important factors • Genetic predisposition • Autoimmune mechanisms • Female sex • 
Smoking • Environmental factors • Hormonal factors • Certain infections may act as 
triggers PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Autoimmune activation ↓ Synovial inflammation ↓ Pannus formation ↓ Cartilage destruction 
↓ Marginal bone erosions ↓ Ligament/tendon damage ↓ Joint instability and deformity CLINICAL FEATURES General • 
Fatigue • Malaise • Fever • Loss of appetite • Weight loss Joint • Symmetrical polyarthritis • Pain • Swelling • Warmth • 
Prolonged morning stiffness typically 30 60 minutes • Reduced ROM Commonly affects • MCP • PIP • Wrist • MTP • Knee • 
Elbow • Shoulder • DIP joints are usually spared CHARACTERISTIC DEFORMITIES Hand • Ulnar deviation • Swan neck 
deformity • Boutonniere deformity • Z thumb deformity • Wrist deformity Foot • Hallux valgus • MTP subluxation • Claw 
toes Cervical spine • Atlantoaxial instability/subluxation COMPLICATIONS Joint • Destruction • Subluxation • Ankylosis • 
Deformity • Disability Extra articular • Rheumatoid nodules • Vasculitis • Interstitial lung disease • Pleural disease • 
Pericarditis • Eye involvement • Anemia • Osteoporosis • Increased cardiovascular risk RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES Early • 
Soft tissue swelling • Periarticular osteopenia Later • Uniform joint space narrowing • Marginal erosions • Subluxation • 
Deformity • Ankylosis in advanced disease Cervical spine • Atlantoaxial instability • Erosive changes CONSERVATIVE 
MANAGEMENT Medical Early treatment with DMARDs is central May include • Methotrexate • Hydroxychloroquine • 
Sulfasalazine • Leflunomide • Biological/targeted DMARDs • NSAIDs • Corticosteroids for selected 
indications Physiotherapy • Pain relief • ROM exercises • Muscle strengthening • Joint protection • Splinting • Energy 
conservation • Hydrotherapy • Functional training • Assistive devices SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Indications • Severe joint 
destruction • Persistent pain • Functional disability • Deformity Procedures • Synovectomy • Tendon repair • Arthrodesis • 
Joint replacement • Cervical stabilization when required --- 3 ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS DEFINITION Ankylosing 
spondylitis AS is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints 
causing inflammatory back pain progressive spinal stiffness and in advanced disease spinal fusion It belongs to the axial
spondyloarthritis spectrum CAUSES / RISK FACTORS • Strong genetic association with HLA B27 • Family history • Immune 
mediated mechanisms • Environmental factors CLINICAL FEATURES Early • Insidious low back pain • Buttock pain • 
Sacroiliac pain • Morning stiffness • Improvement with exercise • Worsening with rest • Night pain Progressive • Reduced 
spinal mobility • Chest expansion • Hip involvement • Fatigue DEFORMITIES Advanced disease may produce • Loss of 
lumbar lordosis • Increased thoracic kyphosis • Forward head posture • Hip flexion deformity • Fixed spinal posture 
Classically described as a bamboo spine in advanced radiographic disease COMPLICATIONS • Severe spinal stiffness • Hip 
arthritis • Osteoporosis • Vertebral fractures • Spinal cord injury after fracture • Uveitis • Cardiovascular involvement • 
Restrictive chest wall mechanics • Functional disability RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES X ray • Sacroiliitis • Vertebral squaring • 
Vertebral corner erosions • Syndesmophytes • Bridging of vertebrae • Bamboo spine • Hip joint changes MRI Can 
demonstrate • Active sacroiliitis • Bone marrow edema • Early inflammatory changes CONSERVATIVE 
MANAGEMENT Medical • NSAIDs • Biologic agents such as TNF inhibitors or IL 17 inhibitors when indicated • Other 
targeted therapy in selected patients Physiotherapy Very important • Spinal mobility exercises • Postural correction • Chest 
expansion exercises • Breathing exercises • Strengthening • Hydrotherapy • Stretching • Aerobic conditioning • Patient 
education • Maintain upright posture • Avoid prolonged flexed posture • Regular exercise SURGICAL 
MANAGEMENT Indications • Severe hip destruction • Fixed severe deformity • Neurological compression • Unstable spinal 
fracture Procedures • Total hip replacement • Corrective spinal osteotomy in selected severe deformities • Spinal 
stabilization/decompression when indicated --- 4 GOUTY ARTHRITIS DEFINITION Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused 
by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues as a result of persistent hyperuricemia CAUSES / RISK 
FACTORS Primary Usually related to impaired uric acid excretion or increased production Secondary • Chronic kidney 
disease • Myeloproliferative disorders • Certain medications • Tumour lysis • High cell turnover Risk factors • Obesity • 
Alcohol excess • High purine diet • Metabolic syndrome • Renal disease • Family history COMMON SITES • First MTP joint 
podagra • Ankle • Knee • Midfoot • Elbow • Wrist • Fingers CLINICAL FEATURES Acute attack • Sudden severe pain • 
Redness • Swelling • Warmth • Extreme tenderness • Often occurs at night Chronic gout • Recurrent attacks • Tophi • Joint 
destruction • Chronic stiffness Tophi Deposits may occur in • Ear • Fingers • Toes • Elbow • Achilles 
tendon COMPLICATIONS • Chronic arthritis • Tophi • Joint destruction • Kidney stones • Chronic kidney disease • Reduced 
function DEFORMITIES • Irregular joint enlargement • Destructive deformity • Tophi related deformity RADIOLOGICAL 
FEATURES X ray • Well defined punched out erosions • Overhanging edges • Preserved joint space until later disease • Soft 
tissue tophi • Bone destruction in advanced disease CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Acute attack • NSAIDs • Colchicine • 
Corticosteroids • Rest and ice • Avoid joint trauma Long term • Weight management • Reduce alcohol • Dietary 
modification • Adequate hydration • Urate lowering therapy ◦ Allopurinol ◦ Febuxostat in appropriate patients • Treatment 
should be individualized based on renal function and comorbidities SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Usually not required May be 
indicated for • Large symptomatic tophi • Nerve compression • Severe joint destruction • Recurrent infection over tophi • 
Severe functional impairment Procedures • Tophus excision • Joint reconstruction/replacement in selected cases --- 5 
PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS DEFINITION Psoriatic arthritis PsA is a chronic inflammatory musculoskeletal disease associated with 
psoriasis involving peripheral joints the axial skeleton entheses and digits CAUSES / RISK FACTORS • Genetic predisposition 
• Psoriasis • Immune dysregulation • Family history • Environmental factors CLINICAL FEATURES Joint • Asymmetrical 
arthritis • Pain • Swelling • Stiffness • Morning stiffness Characteristic • Dactylitis sausage digit • Enthesitis • Commonly ◦ 
Achilles tendon ◦ Plantar fascia Skin • Psoriatic plaques • Nail pitting • Nail dystrophy Spine • Inflammatory back pain in 
axial disease DEFORMITIES • Joint deformity • Flexion deformities • Pencil in cup deformity in severe disease • Arthritis 
mutilans • Ankylosis COMPLICATIONS • Permanent joint damage • Severe functional disability • Spinal stiffness • Eye 
inflammation • Cardiovascular/metabolic comorbidity RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES • Erosions • New bone formation • 
Asymmetric joint space loss • Periostitis • Pencil in cup deformity • Ankylosis • Sacroiliitis • 
Syndesmophytes CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Medical • NSAIDs • DMARDs ◦ Methotrexate ◦ Sulfasalazine in selected 
peripheral disease • Biologic agents • Targeted synthetic DMARDs • Treatment of psoriasis Physiotherapy • ROM exercises 
• Strengthening • Hydrotherapy • Postural exercises • Joint protection • Functional training SURGICAL MANAGEMENT For 
advanced joint destruction • Synovectomy in selected cases • Arthrodesis • Joint replacement • Tendon procedures --- 6 
HAEMOPHILIC ARTHRITIS DEFINITION Haemophilic arthritis is a chronic destructive arthropathy caused by recurrent 
bleeding into joints hemarthrosis in patients with haemophilia It commonly affects • Knee • Ankle • Elbow CAUSE Usually 
occurs in • Hemophilia A factor VIII deficiency • Hemophilia B factor IX deficiency Repeated hemarthroses produce chronic 
synovial inflammation and cartilage destruction PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Factor deficiency ↓ Recurrent hemarthrosis ↓ Blood 
accumulation in joint ↓ Synovial hypertrophy ↓ Iron deposition ↓ Cartilage destruction ↓ Joint space narrowing ↓ 
Deformity CLINICAL FEATURES Acute hemarthrosis • Sudden joint pain • Swelling • Warmth • Restricted movement • 
Protective muscle spasm Chronic • Recurrent swelling • Chronic pain • Stiffness • Muscle wasting • Flexion contractures • 
Reduced ROM DEFORMITIES • Knee flexion deformity • Elbow flexion deformity • Ankle equinus • Joint enlargement • 
Muscle wasting COMPLICATIONS • Chronic arthropathy • Contractures • Joint deformity • Muscle wasting • Secondary 
osteoarthritis • Severe disability • Recurrent bleeding RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES Early • Soft tissue swelling • Joint effusion 
Advanced • Epiphyseal enlargement • Subchondral cysts • Joint space narrowing • Osteophytes • Erosions • Irregular 
articular surfaces MRI can identify • Synovial hypertrophy • Hemosiderin deposition • Cartilage damage CONSERVATIVE 
MANAGEMENT Acute bleed Factor replacement is the main treatment Additional • Rest • Ice • Compression where 
appropriate • Elevation • Analgesia • Protected movement initially Long term • Factor prophylaxis where 
indicated Physiotherapy • Muscle strengthening • ROM exercises • Joint protection • Weight management SURGICAL 
MANAGEMENT For advanced arthropathy • Synovectomy • Joint replacement • Arthroscopic procedures in selected cases 
• Corrective procedures for severe deformity Adequate factor replacement is essential around surgery --- 7 STILLS DISEASE 
/ JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS DEFINITION Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Stills disease is a subtype of juvenile 
idiopathic arthritis characterized by arthritis with systemic inflammation fever and often an evanescent salmon pink 
rash CAUSES Exact cause is unknown Possible mechanisms • Autoinflammatory immune dysfunction • Genetic 
predisposition • Environmental triggers CLINICAL FEATURES Systemic • High spiking fever • Evanescent salmon pink rash • 
Fatigue • Malaise • Lymphadenopathy • Hepatosplenomegaly • Serositis Joint • Pain • Swelling • Stiffness • Reduced ROM 
• Polyarthritis DEFORMITIES Untreated chronic disease may produce • Flexion deformities • Growth disturbance • Limb 
length discrepancy • Joint destruction • Contractures COMPLICATIONS • Growth retardation • Joint destruction • 
Contractures • Osteoporosis • Macrophage activation syndrome • Chronic disability • Amyloidosis in longstanding 
inflammatory disease RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES Early • Soft tissue swelling • Osteopenia Later • Joint space narrowing • 
Growth abnormalities • Erosions • Deformity CONSERVATIVE / MEDICAL MANAGEMENT • NSAIDs • Corticosteroids • 
Methotrexate for persistent arthritis • Biologic agents especially IL 1 or IL 6 targeted therapy where indicated • 
Physiotherapy • Occupational therapy • Nutritional support SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Rarely required in active systemic 
disease In severe chronic joint destruction • Synovectomy in selected cases • Joint replacement • Corrective surgery --- 8 
CHARCOT JOINT DEFINITION Charcot joint neuropathic arthropathy is a progressive destructive arthropathy resulting from 
loss of protective sensation and proprioception leading to repetitive microtrauma joint instability deformity and 
destruction CAUSES Most common • Diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy Other causes • Tabes dorsalis • 
Syringomyelia • Peripheral neuropathy • Spinal cord disease • Congenital sensory neuropathy COMMON SITES • Foot and 
ankle • Midfoot • Knee • Hip • Spine PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Loss of protective sensation ↓ Repeated unrecognized trauma ↓ 
Inflammation + bone resorption ↓ Joint instability ↓ Fragmentation and dislocation ↓ Severe deformity CLINICAL 
FEATURES • Swelling • Warmth • Redness • Instability • Deformity • Reduced pain despite severe structural damage • 
Crepitus • Altered gait Foot • Characteristic rocker bottom deformity may occur COMPLICATIONS • Severe deformity • 
Ulceration • Infection • Osteomyelitis • Amputation • Fractures • Instability • Loss of mobility RADIOLOGICAL 
FEATURES Early • Soft tissue swelling • Subchondral changes Advanced • Joint destruction • Fragmentation • Subluxation • 
Dislocation • Bone sclerosis • Osteophytes • Debris • Deformity A classic description is bag of bones appearance in 
advanced disease CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Acute stage • Complete/off loading as indicated • Total contact casting 
or appropriate immobilization • Custom orthoses • Regular skin inspection • Glycemic control • Foot care 
education Chronic • Custom footwear • Orthoses • Protected weight bearing • Gait training • Fall prevention SURGICAL 
MANAGEMENT Indications • Severe deformity • Instability • Recurrent ulceration • Failure of conservative treatment • 
Severe structural destruction Procedures • Arthrodesis • Corrective osteotomy • Exostectomy in selected cases • 
Reconstruction • Amputation for uncontrollable infection or non reconstructable limb CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISORDERS --
- 9 SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS SLE DEFINITION Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE is a chronic systemic 
autoimmune disease characterized by autoantibody production and immune mediated inflammation affecting multiple 
organs including the skin joints kidneys nervous system blood and cardiovascular system CAUSES / RISK FACTORS • Genetic 
predisposition • Female sex • Hormonal factors • Environmental triggers • Ultraviolet light • Certain medications • 
Infections may act as triggers CLINICAL FEATURES General • Fatigue • Fever • Weight loss Musculoskeletal • Symmetrical 
joint pain • Non erosive inflammatory arthritis • Morning stiffness • Myalgia Skin • Malar rash • Photosensitivity • Discoid 
lesions Other systems • Oral ulcers • Hair loss • Renal disease • Neurological manifestations • Serositis • Hematological 
abnormalities DEFORMITIES Usually non erosive arthritis but chronic disease may cause • Jaccoud arthropathy • Ulnar 
deviation • Swan neck like deformities • Tendon abnormalities These may be partially reducible unlike fixed erosive RA 
deformities COMPLICATIONS • Lupus nephritis • Cardiovascular disease • Stroke • Seizures • Anemia • Thrombocytopenia 
• Osteoporosis • Avascular necrosis particularly with prolonged corticosteroid exposure • Infection RADIOLOGICAL 
FEATURES Usually • Soft tissue swelling • Osteopenia may occur Unlike RA • Marked erosions are usually absent X rays may 
show • Jaccoud type deformities without typical erosive destruction CONSERVATIVE / MEDICAL MANAGEMENT • Patient 
education • Sun protection • Exercise • Hydroxychloroquine in most appropriate patients • NSAIDs for selected 
musculoskeletal symptoms • Corticosteroids for active disease when indicated • Immunosuppressive therapy • Biologic 
therapy in selected patients • Treatment of individual organ involvement SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Not usually directed at 
SLE itself May be required for • Severe joint destruction • Avascular necrosis • Fracture • Tendon deformity Procedures • 
Joint replacement • Corrective surgery • Fracture fixation --- 10 SCLERODERMA / SYSTEMIC 
SCLEROSIS DEFINITION Systemic sclerosis scleroderma is a chronic autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by 
vascular abnormalities immune dysregulation and excessive collagen deposition resulting in fibrosis and hardening of skin 
and potentially internal organs TYPES 1 Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis Skin involvement mainly distal to 
elbows/knees and face 2 Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis More extensive skin involvement including trunk and 
proximal limbs CAUSES / RISK FACTORS Exact cause unknown Factors • Genetic predisposition • Autoimmune mechanisms 
• Environmental exposures • Vascular dysfunction CLINICAL FEATURES Skin • Skin thickening • Tight shiny skin • Loss of 
skin folds • Reduced mobility Hands • Raynaud phenomenon • Puffy fingers initially • Sclerodactyly • Digital ulcers • 
Contractures Face • Tight facial skin • Reduced mouth opening • Mask like appearance Systemic • Dysphagia • Reflux • 
Interstitial lung disease • Pulmonary hypertension • Renal crisis DEFORMITIES • Flexion contractures of fingers • 
Sclerodactyly • Reduced mouth opening • Hand deformity • Joint stiffness COMPLICATIONS • Digital ulcers • Gangrene • 
Pulmonary fibrosis • Pulmonary hypertension • Renal crisis • Cardiac disease • Esophageal dysfunction • Severe functional 
disability RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES May show • Soft tissue calcification • Acro osteolysis • Joint space changes • 
Contractures Chest imaging may demonstrate • Interstitial lung disease/fibrosis CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Medical • 
Vasodilator therapy for Raynaud phenomenon • Immunosuppressive therapy for selected systemic disease • Proton pump 
inhibitors for reflux • Treatment of pulmonary hypertension • Renal blood pressure management Physiotherapy • ROM 
exercises • Stretching • Hand exercises • Splinting when indicated • Breathing exercises • Aerobic conditioning • Functional 
training • Skin protection and education SURGICAL MANAGEMENT May include • Debridement of severe digital ulcers • 
Management of gangrene • Joint reconstruction in selected cases • Surgical treatment of severe contractures --- 11 
DERMATOMYOSITIS DEFINITION Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized by proximal 
skeletal muscle weakness and characteristic cutaneous manifestations CAUSES / RISK FACTORS Exact cause unknown 
Possible associations • Autoimmune predisposition • Genetic factors • Environmental triggers • In some adults association 
with malignancy CLINICAL FEATURES Muscle • Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness • Difficulty climbing stairs • 
Difficulty rising from a chair • Difficulty lifting arms • Difficulty combing hair • Neck flexor weakness Skin • Heliotrope rash 
• Gottron papules • Photosensitive rash • Shawl sign • V sign Other • Dysphagia • Respiratory muscle involvement • 
Fatigue DEFORMITIES / FUNCTIONAL PROBLEMS • Flexion contractures • Poor posture • Muscle wasting • Reduced 
mobility • Difficulty with transfers • Gait abnormalities • Children may develop calcinosis COMPLICATIONS • Severe muscle 
weakness • Dysphagia • Aspiration • Respiratory failure • Interstitial lung disease • Calcinosis • Malignancy association in 
some adults • Disability RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES There are no characteristic plain X ray findings MRI muscle may show • 
Muscle edema • Inflammatory changes • Muscle atrophy in chronic disease Other investigations • Elevated CK • EMG 
abnormalities • Muscle biopsy in selected cases CONSERVATIVE / MEDICAL MANAGEMENT Medical • Corticosteroids • 
Immunosuppressive agents • IVIG in selected cases • Other immunomodulatory/biologic therapies as appropriate • Sun 
protection • Treatment of dysphagia and respiratory complications Physiotherapy • Gentle ROM • Gradual strengthening 
after disease control • Aerobic conditioning • Functional training • Energy conservation • Respiratory exercises where 
indicated • Avoid aggressive exercise during uncontrolled active myositis SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Usually not required 
for the primary disease May be required for • Severe calcinosis • Contractures • Secondary complications --- 12 
POLIOMYELITIS Important Poliomyelitis is primarily an infectious viral disease of the nervous system not a connective 
tissue disease It is included here because it is part of the requested syllabus DEFINITION Poliomyelitis is an acute viral 
infection caused by poliovirus primarily affecting the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and sometimes the brainstem 
resulting in flaccid muscle weakness or paralysis CAUSE Causative organism • Poliovirus Transmission • Mainly fecal oral 
route • Occasionally oral oral transmission PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Poliovirus infection ↓ Viral replication ↓ CNS invasion in 
severe disease ↓ Anterior horn cell destruction ↓ Lower motor neuron dysfunction ↓ Flaccid paralysis CLINICAL 
FEATURES Prodromal • Fever • Headache • Malaise • Sore throat • Vomiting Paralytic disease • Acute asymmetric 
weakness • Flaccid paralysis • Reduced muscle tone • Reduced/absent reflexes • Muscle wasting • Fasciculations may 
occur • Sensory function usually preserved Respiratory involvement • Intercostal weakness • Diaphragmatic weakness • 
Respiratory failure DEFORMITIES Long term sequelae may include • Equinus deformity • Knee flexion deformity • Hip 
deformity • Scoliosis • Limb shortening • Foot deformity • Joint contractures COMPLICATIONS • Respiratory failure • 
Aspiration • Permanent paralysis • Muscle wasting • Contractures • Skeletal deformity • Post polio syndrome years later • 
Reduced functional independence RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES X rays are not diagnostic of acute poliomyelitis Chronic cases 
may show • Muscle wasting related osteopenia • Limb shortening • Deformities • Scoliosis • Joint 
contractures CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT Acute • Supportive medical care • Respiratory support • Pain control • 
Prevention of contractures • Appropriate positioning Rehabilitation • ROM exercises • Muscle strengthening of functioning 
muscles • Orthoses • Gait training • Energy conservation • Assistive devices • Respiratory physiotherapy where 
indicated Post polio syndrome • Pacing • Energy conservation • Avoid overuse weakness • Appropriate low to moderate 
exercise • Functional adaptation SURGICAL MANAGEMENT For residual deformities • Tendon transfer • Corrective 
osteotomy • Arthrodesis • Limb length procedures in selected cases • Spinal surgery for severe scoliosis • Orthopaedic 
reconstruction --- 13 MIXED CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISEASE MCTD DEFINITION Mixed connective tissue disease MCTD is an 
autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by overlapping clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus 
systemic sclerosis polymyositis/dermatomyositis and rheumatoid arthritis usually associated with high levels of anti U1 RNP 
antibodies CAUSES Exact cause is unknown Associated with • Genetic predisposition • Autoimmune dysregulation • 
Environmental triggers CLINICAL FEATURES Musculoskeletal • Polyarthritis • Arthralgia • Myalgia • Proximal muscle 
weakness Vascular • Raynaud phenomenon Skin • Puffy fingers • Sclerodactyly like changes • Rash Other • Dysphagia • 
Esophageal dysfunction • Interstitial lung disease • Pulmonary hypertension • Fatigue DEFORMITIES May develop • Joint 
deformity • Contractures • Sclerodactyly • Muscle wasting • Reduced hand function COMPLICATIONS • Pulmonary 
hypertension • Interstitial lung disease • Esophageal dysfunction • Cardiac involvement • Renal involvement usually less 
prominent than in classic SLE • Severe muscle weakness • Functional disability RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES No single 
pathognomonic radiographic appearance May demonstrate • Joint space narrowing • Soft tissue swelling • Erosive arthritis 
in some patients • Interstitial lung disease on chest X ray/HRCT • Muscle inflammation/edema on 
MRI INVESTIGATIONS Blood • ANA • Anti U1 RNP • CBC • ESR/CRP • CK • Renal and liver function Other • Pulmonary 
function tests • Echocardiography • HRCT chest where indicated • MRI muscle if myositis is suspected CONSERVATIVE / 
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT Treatment depends on the dominant manifestations May include • NSAIDs • Corticosteroids • 
Hydroxychloroquine • Methotrexate • Other immunosuppressive drugs • Vasodilators for Raynaud phenomenon • 
Treatment for pulmonary hypertension • Treatment of interstitial lung disease Physiotherapy • ROM exercises • Muscle 
strengthening • Aerobic conditioning • Breathing exercises • Hand therapy • Joint protection • Energy conservation • 
Functional training SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Usually not required for the primary disease May be considered for • Severe 
joint destruction • Fixed deformity • Contractures • Digital complications • Joint replacement in selected cases
CO 5 -- 1 CERVICOBRACHIAL SYNDROME Definition Cervicobrachial syndrome is a clinical condition characterized by pain 
paraesthesia numbness weakness or other neurological symptoms originating from the cervical spine or surrounding 
structures and radiating into the shoulder arm forearm or hand Causes / Etiology • Cervical intervertebral disc prolapse • 
Cervical spondylosis and osteophytes • Foraminal or spinal canal stenosis • Whiplash and other cervical trauma • Muscle 
spasm and postural dysfunction • Brachial plexus lesions • Tumour infection or inflammatory disorders • Thoracic outlet 
disorders Pathophysiology Cervical pathology → nerve root irritation/compression → inflammation and impaired nerve 
conduction → pain and paraesthesia → weakness and functional limitation Clinical Features • Neck pain with radiation to 
shoulder/upper limb • Burning shooting or electric shock like pain • Paraesthesia and numbness in a dermatomal pattern • 
'''

def process(t):
    t = t.replace('•', '-')
    # regex to find caps words, like DEFINITION, TYPES, CLINICAL FEATURES, etc. and wrap them in ** **
    # words that are all caps and length > 2
    # Be careful not to wrap random things. 
    # Better to just use regex to replace specific known headers.
    headers = [
        'PHYSIOTHERAPY', 'DEFINITION', 'TYPES', 'RISK FACTORS', 'PATHOPHYSIOLOGY', 'CLINICAL FEATURES',
        'INVESTIGATIONS', 'COMPLICATIONS', 'MEDICAL MANAGEMENT', 'SURGICAL MANAGEMENT', 'PHYSIOTHERAPY MANAGEMENT',

- Fever
- Headache
- Malaise
- Sore throat
- Vomiting Paralytic disease
- Acute asymmetric 
weakness
- Flaccid paralysis
- Reduced muscle tone

- Muscle wasting

occur

- Intercostal weakness

- Equinus deformity
- Knee flexion deformity
- Hip 
deformity

- Limb shortening
- Foot deformity
- Joint contractures **COMPLICATIONS**
- Respiratory failure
- Aspiration
- Permanent paralysis
- Muscle wasting
- Contractures

- Reduced functional independence **RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES** X rays are not diagnostic of acute poliomyelitis Chronic cases 
may show
- Muscle wasting related osteopenia
- Limb shortening
- Deformities
- Scoliosis
- Joint 
contractures **CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT** Acute
- Supportive medical care
- Respiratory support
- Pain control
- Prevention of contractures
- Appropriate positioning Rehabilitation
- ROM exercises
- Muscle strengthening of functioning 
muscles
- Orthoses
- Gait training
- Energy conservation
- Assistive devices
- Respiratory physiotherapy where 
indicated Post polio syndrome
- Pacing
- Energy conservation
- Avoid overuse weakness
- Appropriate low to moderate 
exercise

- Tendon transfer
- Corrective 
osteotomy

reconstruction --- 13 **MIXED CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISEASE MCTD DEFINITION** Mixed connective tissue disease MCTD is an 
autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by overlapping clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus 
systemic sclerosis polymyositis/dermatomyositis and rheumatoid arthritis usually associated with high levels of anti U1 RNP 
antibodies **CAUSES** Exact cause is unknown Associated with
- Genetic predisposition
- Autoimmune dysregulation
- Environmental triggers **CLINICAL FEATURES** Musculoskeletal
- Polyarthritis
- Arthralgia
- Myalgia
- Proximal muscle 
weakness Vascular
- Raynaud phenomenon Skin
- Puffy fingers
- Sclerodactyly like changes
- Rash Other
- Dysphagia
- Esophageal dysfunction
- Interstitial lung disease
- Pulmonary hypertension
- Fatigue **DEFORMITIES** May develop
- Joint 
deformity
- Contractures
- Sclerodactyly
- Muscle wasting
- Reduced hand function **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pulmonary 
hypertension
- Interstitial lung disease
- Esophageal dysfunction
- Cardiac involvement
- Renal involvement usually less 
prominent than in classic SLE
- Severe muscle weakness
- Functional disability **RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES** No single 
pathognomonic radiographic appearance May demonstrate
- Joint space narrowing
- Soft tissue swelling

in some patients

function tests

joint destruction

CO 5 -- 1 **CERVICOBRACHIAL SYNDROME Definition** Cervicobrachial syndrome is a clinical condition characterized by pain 
paraesthesia numbness weakness or other neurological symptoms originating from the cervical spine or surrounding 
structures and radiating into the shoulder arm forearm or hand **Causes / Etiology**
- Cervical intervertebral disc prolapse
- Cervical spondylosis and osteophytes
- Foraminal or spinal canal stenosis
- Whiplash and other cervical trauma
- Muscle 
spasm and postural dysfunction
- Brachial plexus lesions
- Tumour infection or inflammatory disorders
- Thoracic outlet 
disorders **Pathophysiology** Cervical pathology → nerve root irritation/compression → inflammation and impaired nerve 
conduction → pain and paraesthesia → weakness and functional limitation **Clinical Features**
- Neck pain with radiation to 
shoulder/upper limb
- Burning shooting or electric shock like pain
- Paraesthesia and numbness in a dermatomal pattern
